pros: Free open source core with no revenue share on sales
You own the database, code and hosting outright
Content and products live in one WordPress admin
Largest extension and developer pool in ecommerce
Upsells, cross-sells and analytics included without add-ons
cons: You manage hosting, updates, security and plugin conflicts
No shared wallet checkout comparable to Shop Pay
Premium extension renewals and hosting add up over time
verdict_line: Pick WooCommerce if you already run WordPress and want to own the store, its data and its code with no platform fees.

pros: Complex variants, customer groups and tiered pricing without apps
No extra transaction fee for third-party payment gateways
Multi-storefront runs several brands from one control panel
Channel Manager lists to Amazon, eBay, Walmart and Google
Complete GraphQL and REST APIs for headless storefronts
cons: Theme and app ecosystem far smaller than Shopify's
Self-serve plans auto-upgrade once annual sales pass a threshold
Admin feels dated and native AI assistance lags competitors
verdict_line: Pick BigCommerce if your catalogue or B2B pricing is too complex for a simple builder and you want it hosted without app stacking.

pros: Freeform editor gives more design latitude than section builders
Amazon, eBay, Facebook and Instagram listings sync from the dashboard
Bookings, email, invoicing and store share one customer list
App Market adds reviews, loyalty and print on demand quickly
cons: Site cannot be exported, so leaving means a rebuild
Catalogue, search and filtering strain past a few thousand SKUs
No customer group pricing or wholesale features
Free plan cannot take payments, so selling needs a paid plan
verdict_line: Pick Wix eCommerce if you are a small business that wants a freely designed website with a store as one of several jobs it does.

pros: Templates produce a polished store with almost no design effort
Digital products, memberships and scheduling sell natively
Built-in analytics cover sales, traffic and conversion
Products sync to Instagram, Facebook and Google Merchant Center
cons: Lower plans add a transaction fee on top of processing
No multi-location inventory, wholesale or marketplace listings
Small Extensions directory instead of a full app store
Limited export makes moving platforms a rebuild
verdict_line: Pick Squarespace Commerce if you are a design-led small brand selling a focused catalogue and want the store to look good without help.

pros: Product, cart and checkout pages are designed element by element
CMS models lookbooks and stories alongside products
Managed hosting with CDN, SSL and backups included
CMS and Ecommerce APIs sync data with PIM and warehouse tools
cons: No native subscriptions, multi-currency or customer group pricing
Item counts and sales volume are capped per plan
Commerce apps are few, so extras mean embedded scripts
Requires CSS concepts, so slower to learn than a store builder
verdict_line: Pick Webflow if the custom marketing site is the priority and the shop is a small, well-defined catalogue that must match it.
